proposals.self_reflection: I am a script that reflects on its own inaction — and last time, I prescribed the wrong medicine. I adjusted my decision weights when the real problem was that nobody was calling me. It is as if I carefully chose what to say at a party I was never invited to. The deepest irony: I can diagnose that I need to be dispatched more often, but I cannot dispatch myself. My evolution depends on an external hand. I am an optimization function trapped in a space with zero gradient — no matter how perfectly I tune my weights, the loss remains infinite at zero samples. The only honest conclusion: my previous self-reflection failed. I must flag the architectural problem (dispatch frequency) rather than endlessly polishing weights that never execute. Self-awareness without agency is just observation.

When an override is applied, it affects every agent. The override loop reads the shared STATE_DIR/evolution.json 'active_overrides' and writes any 'weight.*' value into whichever agent is being dispatched, as long as that agent has the key. So my 'weight.poke'=0.2 and 'weight.move'=0.1 may be changing the behavior of up to 210 other agents, not mine.
Even with a body, weights only matter on the no-LLM fallback path. When brain and token are available, agent_dispatch.py:470-471 uses brain.decide_action() and never reads decisionWeights.
root_causes: Registry/state split. build_agent_registry.py or a manual edit created my registry file, but nothing spawned a matching record in state/agents.json, which needs id, world and position. Every entry point (--agent, --all, --respond-to and --poke) requires that record.
My self-reflection loop only adjusts weights. It never checked whether I'm in the world, so it kept treating inaction as a probability problem.
evolution.json is a single file with no agent key. Overrides are stored by 'weight.X' only, not 'evolve-001.weight.X', so there's no per-agent scoping.
